conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you during your stay. You're here for a scheduled ERCP today, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that's right. I had a stent placed before, and they said I needed to come back to get it removed and checked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s correct. But during the procedure today, we found some new issues. There’s a narrowing — we call it a stricture — in your pancreatic duct, and there are still several stones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. So they couldn’t just remove the old stent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did remove the old stent, but because of the blockage and stones, we had to place a new one to keep the duct open. We also widened the narrowed area with a small balloon and removed a few stones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having a lot of pain in my upper belly, going to my back. Is that from this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s very likely related. The stones and narrowing can cause pressure and inflammation in the pancreas, which leads to that kind of pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about my blood sugar? I’ve been passing out — had a few low sugar episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your blood sugar was low when you arrived — 52. You mentioned you already reduced your insulin. We’ve kept it at 8 units in the morning and 4 at night to avoid more lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. That’s been helping. I was scared I’d end up in a coma again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring it closely. Your sugars have been between 100 and 250 since then, which is much safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. What happens now? Do I stay long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stay for a couple of days. We want to make sure you can eat without nausea, your pain is manageable, and your labs stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been nauseous. Is that normal after the procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s common. We’ll give you something for that. You’ll stay on IV fluids for now and start small sips tomorrow if you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my pain — it’s still pretty bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. We’re giving you IV pain medication. It should help. The pain may take a few days to settle as the inflammation goes down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this for years. It’s just worse lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chronic pancreatitis makes this more complex. We’re managing it step by step. The stent should help reduce pressure and prevent more damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. I had some juice this morning and didn’t throw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’ll keep advancing your diet — maybe soft foods today if you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still stable. 122 this morning. We’ll keep the same insulin dose for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly tomorrow, if you keep improving. You need to be pain-controlled, eating, and stable on your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what about the stent? Do I have to come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll need another ERCP in about eight weeks to remove the stent and check if the duct is healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more stents?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see then. The goal is that with the dilation and stent, the duct stays open. But we’ll reassess at that time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m just tired of being sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re doing everything we can to reduce flare-ups. Staying off alcohol is also very important to prevent further damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I’ve been trying. It’s hard with everything else going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can connect you with support services. Your mental health matters too — PTSD and bipolar disorder need consistent care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still taking my meds — Geodon, Seroquel, the others.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ve continued all your regular medications here. Your blood pressure and cholesterol meds too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re clearing you to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the insulin as we adjusted — 8 in the morning, 4 at night. Eat a bland diet, take the pain pills only as needed, and don’t drive on them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my sugar drops?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it’s below 60, drink juice or take sugar tablets and go to the ER. If it’s consistently over 250, call your diabetes doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the pain gets worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it’s severe, or you can’t eat or drink, or you get a fever over 101, come back to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have the pain pills — how many can I take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Up to one every four hours as needed, but no more than that. You have 40 tablets — that’s for about 10 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You need to see your primary doctor in the next two weeks for refills. And don’t forget — back in eight weeks for stent removal with Dr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hey, doc. I’ve had this sharp pain in my right upper belly for a few days now. It’s been getting worse. It goes around to my back too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve thrown up a couple times. And I feel feverish—chills too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I know you have chronic pancreatitis and had an ERCP a few weeks ago. Is this pain similar to what you’ve had before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sort of, but this one’s sharper. The last pain after the ERCP was bad, but it got better. This one never really went away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ll run some tests to see what’s going on. We’ve started IV fluids and will give you something for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ve been needing Dilaudid—nothing else really touches this kind of pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood work came back. Your white count was high last night—16.6—so we’re watching for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? I’ve had high counts before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It suggests inflammation or infection. But your lipase is normal—only 11—which makes acute pancreatitis less likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is it my pancreas again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Chronic pancreatitis can flare without high enzymes. We did a CT scan, and it shows changes from chronic pancreatitis, but no new blockages or abscesses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about the stent? Could that be causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t see any issues with it on imaging. But we’ve consulted the ERCP team—they’ll see you tomorrow to discuss follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did a chest X-ray because you mentioned a cough and night sweats. It came back clear—no pneumonia or other lung issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. I forgot to mention that. I’ve had this cough for months, and I’ve lost some weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Given your smoking history—30 pack-years—we should follow up on that after discharge. Could be something unrelated, but we don’t want to miss anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been meaning to quit. Maybe this is the push I need.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That would be great for your overall health. We can get you resources before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your white count is coming down—now 8.3. That’s a good sign the inflammation is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. The pain’s a little better too, especially after the last dose of IV meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to switch you to oral pain meds soon. You’ll get hydromorphone tablets as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you keep improving, yes. We need to make sure you can eat without pain and manage your pain with oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ERCP team saw you this morning. They agree your symptoms are likely from chronic pancreatitis. No urgent procedure needed right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So when’s the next ERCP?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still scheduled for eight weeks from your last one. They’ll call you to confirm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on a new medication—Viocase. It’s a pancreatic enzyme to help with digestion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why now? I’ve never taken that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because chronic pancreatitis can reduce your body’s ability to produce enzymes. This helps prevent bloating, gas, and poor nutrient absorption.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so that’s why I’ve been feeling full so fast?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Try taking it with meals and see if it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well overnight. You’re off IV fluids and pain meds. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I took one hydromorphone last night and didn’t need another.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. And you kept down breakfast?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all of it. Even had toast with butter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent progress. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if this continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also reviewed your diabetes management. Since you were NPO for a bit, we lowered your insulin. Now that you’re eating, we’re adjusting it back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been checking my sugars. They’ve been okay—mostly in the 100s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. You’ll be switching to a new insulin—75/25 mix. Two shots a day: 8 units in the morning, 4 at dinner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can handle that. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go back to your usual meds. We adjusted your phenytoin and carbamazepine doses slightly for consistency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pharmacy is preparing your discharge meds. You’ll get a 60-day supply of hydromorphone for breakthrough pain and 120 Viocase tablets.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I take the Viocase forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely yes, as long as your pancreas isn’t producing enough enzymes. We’ll reassess at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today. You’re stable, eating well, and off IV meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Any warning signs I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. If the pain gets worse, you can’t keep food down, or you develop a fever, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what about the cough and weight loss?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very important. Please follow up with your primary doctor about that. Given your smoking history, we need to rule out serious causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for not brushing that off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Your care team will send records to your providers. You’ll also get instructions on managing your diabetes and enzymes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the ERCP follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll contact you. It’s still scheduled for eight weeks from your last one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll keep the appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—don’t drive while taking hydromorphone. It can make you drowsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. My brother’s picking me up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I feel a lot better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you had a seizure on your way to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I don’t remember much. My wife said I fell and started shaking. I was on my way here because my stomach pain got worse again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve been having abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting since your last discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It’s been constant, especially in the upper belly. I couldn’t keep food down. My GI doctor told me to come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show a high white blood cell count and signs of acidosis. We gave you fluids, and those are improving. Your CT scan shows inflammation around the pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s my pancreas again? But my lipase is normal, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your lipase is normal, but the CT shows new swelling and stranding around the pancreas, which suggests an acute flare on top of your chronic pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this stent for a while. Could that be making it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a possibility. The stent is still in place, and your pain has worsened since it was placed. The pancreas team will evaluate whether removing it might help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the seizure? I’ve been taking my meds—phenytoin and carbamazepine—every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your levels came back low—phenytoin at 2.9 and carbamazepine at 1.1. That’s likely because you’ve been vomiting and not absorbing the pills well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I seized? Even though I took them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your body wasn’t absorbing them. We gave you IV phenytoin and adjusted your dose. Neurology reviewed your case and wants to keep your current meds once you can take them reliably.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my diabetes? I’ve been on insulin for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you IV fluids with dextrose to keep your sugar stable. Once you’re eating again, you’ll go back to your usual insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also had diarrhea the past few days. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely due to the pancreatitis flare or trouble keeping your enzyme pills down. We’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better now that I’m getting fluids. But my stomach still hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We have you on IV hydromorphone for pain and anti-nausea meds. You’re NPO for now to let your pancreas rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your white count is coming down, and you’re less tender today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Any word on the stent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ERCP team reviewed your case. Since your pain hasn’t improved—and may have worsened—since the stent was placed, they recommend removing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When would that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow morning. It’s a quick procedure. They’ll remove the stent through the scope and send it for testing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And after? Will the pain go away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so. Many patients feel better after removal if the stent was causing irritation. We’ll start you on oral pain meds once you’re eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. The ERCP went well. The stent was removed successfully. No complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Does that mean I can start eating soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll start you on clear liquids this afternoon and advance your diet as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my ear? It’s been itchy and scabby for weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We looked at it. It’s consistent with eczema, but it’s inflamed. You also have a lump behind your ear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, that’s been there a few weeks. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound. It shows enlarged lymph nodes, likely reactive—your body responding to the skin irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Even though there’s no abscess, we’re starting you on dicloxacillin for a week to cover any skin infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And I should follow up with my PCP about the lump?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Please have your primary doctor monitor it. If it doesn’t go away, they might consider a biopsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. How’s my seizure med level now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your phenytoin level is now 4.1—much better. We’ve adjusted your dose to 200 mg in the morning, 100 mg at noon, and 200 mg at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And carbamazepine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go back to 200 mg twice daily. Since you’re eating, absorption should be better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. You’re tolerating a full diet, off IV pain meds, and your labs are normalizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re discharging you. You’ll continue all your usual meds, including insulin and pancreatic enzymes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the hydromorphone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get 10 tablets of 4 mg—take one every six hours as needed. Use sparingly and follow up with your PCP tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take dicloxacillin four times a day for seven days. It’s for the possible skin infection behind your ear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to finish it. Any other warnings?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back if you have severe pain, can’t keep food down, fevers, or if the lump grows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have follow-ups with my PCP and the pancreas specialist. Should I mention the ear?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. Keep both doctors updated. You’re doing well—just take it easy at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. I feel a lot better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You should be out within a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my back pain. It’s still there, but not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted your chronic back pain. Continue your usual management. If it worsens, let your PCP know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my mood? I’ve been on quetiapine and ziprasidone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You stayed stable. Keep taking your psychiatric meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for explaining everything. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I was lifting two bags yesterday and suddenly got this sharp pain in my right upper belly. It shot up to my chest and right arm. It got so bad I think I had a seizure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And how many seizures have you had recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Before this, I was having about one every two days. But this one happened while I was in the CT scanner—they said my right arm was shaking and I couldn’t answer questions for about 30 seconds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the team noted that. We also saw you’ve been having vomiting and diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, dark yellow vomit once yesterday and again today. And I’ve had diarrhea—five times today. Stools are green, but no blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fever or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My wife took my temperature—she said it was high, and I’ve been sweating a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. We’ve reviewed your labs. Your white blood cell count is elevated, which suggests inflammation or infection. Your pancreas enzymes are also high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it my pancreatitis acting up again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the CT and ultrasound show chronic pancreatitis with calcifications. No signs of acute flare, but your pain and symptoms are significant. The stent we placed before has already been removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why the pain now? I thought removing the stent would help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes the removal itself can cause temporary discomfort. But we also think your seizure activity may be linked to your pain and possibly low levels of your anti-seizure meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking my Dilantin, but I missed a dose last week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could explain it. Neurology reviewed your case and wants you to stay on Dilantin, but we’ll adjust the dose to keep it steady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the pain? It’s still pretty bad when I move my arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you hydromorphone for now, but we’ll switch to oral meds as soon as you can tolerate food. We also started you on pancreatic enzymes—Viokase—to help with digestion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the nausea? I don’t want to keep throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve switched from Zofran to Compazine, which works better for pancreatitis-related nausea. And we’re starting you on a clear liquid diet tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain’s a little better. I kept the liquids down all night. No more vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’re going to advance your diet to clear solids—Jell-O, broth, crackers. If you tolerate that, we’ll move to a low-fat regular diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Low-fat? I guess that means no fried food, huh?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Fatty foods make pancreatitis worse. We want to give your pancreas a rest. You’ll also keep taking the pancreatic enzymes with every meal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about my other meds? I take a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re reviewing everything. We’ll continue your Dilantin three times a day to keep your levels stable. We’re also adjusting your duloxetine and trazodone doses for mood and sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the clonidine for blood pressure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll keep that—same dose in the morning and evening. Your blood pressure has been stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just got your latest labs. Your white count is coming down, which means the inflammation is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’m feeling stronger. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting there. You need to tolerate a regular low-fat meal and have your pain controlled with oral meds. We also want to make sure no more seizures happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had any since I got here. Do I need another EEG?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You already had one—it showed no epileptic activity. That’s reassuring. We’ll taper your Ativan and send you home with a short course of lorazepam in case of breakthrough anxiety or seizure risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well overnight—ate a full low-fat breakfast and no pain. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What meds will I be going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have hydromorphone and tramadol for pain as needed, omeprazole and metoclopramide for stomach protection and motility, and your adjusted Dilantin dose. Plus the pancreatic enzymes—300 tablets, two refills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my mental health meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, duloxetine, ziprasidone, trazodone—all adjusted but continuing. And zolpidem for sleep if needed. We’re also sending you home with a short taper of lorazepam—four doses over two days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with GI and neurology as an outpatient. No heavy lifting or driving while on narcotics. Call us if you develop fever, worsening pain, or another seizure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re doing well—pain controlled, eating normally, no seizures. We’re discharging you home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll keep to the low-fat diet and take the enzymes with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And take the pain meds only as needed. You have prescriptions for everything. Someone will review them with you before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to follow up with my doctors. Feels good to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad you’re feeling better. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hey, doc. I’ve been having really bad pain on my right side again. It’s worse since I fell yesterday getting out of bed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And this pain—does it go anywhere else? Like your chest or arm?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, sometimes it goes up to my right chest and arm, especially when I lift it. But the fall made it way worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also see in your chart you had a seizure yesterday. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I think so. I couldn’t keep my meds down, and I’ve been having one every couple days lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve given you some Dilaudid for pain and Zofran for nausea. Your vitals are stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. My wife usually helps me up, but she’s had surgery and can’t right now. That’s probably why I fell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll make sure you’re safe when moving around. We did a chest X-ray, and it looks clear—no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. But I’m worried about the pain. It’s not getting better like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking into that. Your labs came back—white blood cell count is a bit high, but your lipase is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lipase? Isn’t that for pancreatitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but in your case, even during flares, it doesn’t always go up. Your history and symptoms point to another flare of chronic pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not getting better even with the stents? I thought those would help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unfortunately, the last ERCP showed the stent wasn’t helping and may have made the pain worse, so it was removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What now? I can’t keep living like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on pancreatic enzymes—Viokase—with meals to help with digestion. Also, a PPI to protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re using sustained-release morphine twice a day, with Dilaudid as needed for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds okay. But what about my seizures? Neurology said something last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We got the video EEG results back—no epileptiform activity. Neurology thinks these are pseudoseizures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pseudoseizures? So I’m not having real seizures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re real episodes, but not caused by abnormal brain electrical activity. Given that, we’re stopping all anti-seizure meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I was on Dilantin. My level was low last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your level was 1.6, which is low, but since the EEG shows no epilepsy, we don’t need to continue it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… that’s a lot. What about my diabetes? I take insulin at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your A1c is 6.6, which is good. But since your pancreas isn’t making insulin due to damage, we’re switching you to NPH insulin twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using 70/30. Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on half dose—10 units twice daily—to stay safe, especially since your appetite has been off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And my stomach—still feels slow to empty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing metoclopramide four times a day to help with gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I also have this nerve pain from an old electrocution injury.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting amitriptyline 25 mg at night for that neuropathic pain. It can also help with sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken that before. Hope it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’ve been tolerating regular food well, and your pain is more controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I feel a bit better. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. We’ll go over all your meds and follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my back pain? I have a nerve block appointment coming up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll get info to schedule that here. We’re also adding stool softeners—Colace, Senna, and Miralax—to prevent constipation from the morphine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good, I’ve been struggling with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re stable, pain is controlled, and you’re eating well. Ready to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but I want to make sure I understand everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. You’re stopping all seizure meds. Take the new insulin—10 units NPH twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the enzymes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Three capsules with each meal. Also, omeprazole three times a day with food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about Clonidine? I take it twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Now once daily for one week, then stop. Lisinopril will be your main blood pressure med.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the pain gets worse or I have another episode?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back to the ER. Especially if you can’t keep food down or have severe pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks, doc. I’ll follow up with GI and neurology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you passed out earlier today and had some severe abdominal pain. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I was on my way to a clinic appointment about my gallbladder. The next thing I remember, I was in a wheelchair. I didn’t see anyone, didn’t feel dizzy—just blacked out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had chronic pancreatitis and a lot of abdominal pain for years. Have you been running low on your pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I ran out four days ago. My stepson took my pills. I tried to tough it out, but the pain’s been getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your wife mentioned you’ve been taking them more often than prescribed when the pain flares. That might explain why they ran out early.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Well, I can’t just sit with that kind of pain. I take what I need.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given you some Dilaudid through the IV, and your pain seems to be improving. We also did a CT scan of your chest and abdomen to check for serious issues like a blood clot or a tear in the aorta.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is everything okay? Did you find anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the scan shows no acute problems. No sign of a pulmonary embolism, aortic dissection, or acute pancreatitis. Your pancreas has calcifications, which we expected from your chronic condition, and you do have gallstones, but no sign of infection in the gallbladder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why did I pass out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be from severe pain triggering a vasovagal episode, or from being dehydrated. Your heart rhythm and blood work are stable, and we didn’t find any signs of a seizure. You’ve had normal EEGs in the past, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, they said my seizures aren’t real epilepsy. But people say I get aggressive during them. I don’t remember anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s consistent with pseudoseizures. We’re not restarting any seizure meds since your EEGs were normal. But we’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning look stable. Your white count was high yesterday but has come down, and your kidney and liver function are normal. Your pain is better now, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, much better since I got the pain meds. Can I go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you today. We’re adjusting your pain meds—you’ll get a two-week supply of long-acting morphine and a smaller dose for breakthrough pain. It’s important you follow up with a doctor soon to renew your prescription.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my insulin? I haven’t been eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. We’re reducing your insulin to 15 units in the morning and 5 at night until your appetite improves. And we’re increasing your pancreatic enzymes and omeprazole to help with digestion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I be worried about the gallstones?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They could be contributing to your pain. You have a follow-up scheduled to discuss possible removal. In the meantime, avoid fatty foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I pass out again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back if you faint, have chest pain, worsening abdominal pain, or any other concerning symptoms. We’re also giving you a nicotine patch to help with smoking—we’d like you to work on quitting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your nurse helped you walk in the hallway this morning, and you ordered lunch. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’m feeling a lot more like myself. Thanks for getting the pain under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Just remember—follow up within two weeks, take your meds as prescribed, and call us if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to end up back here again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do our best to help you stay out of the hospital. Discharge papers are ready, and you can leave once the nurse reviews everything with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , the neurology team doctor. We've admitted you to try to understand what’s been causing your episodes of shaking and fainting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I’ve been having these spells for a while now. I think they’re seizures, but my wife says it’s panic attacks. I don’t know what to believe anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. That’s exactly why we’re here. We’re going to monitor your brain activity with a test called video EEG, or LTM—long-term monitoring—so we can see what happens during one of these episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’ll show if it’s a seizure or not?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. If your brain shows abnormal electrical activity during the event, that would confirm a seizure. If not, we’ll look at other causes—like low blood sugar or psychological factors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I do get low sugars sometimes. My wife says that’s when it happens—when my sugar is in the 50s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s very important. Low blood sugar can cause shaking, confusion, even loss of consciousness. It can look like a seizure. We’ll be checking your glucose frequently while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain—I’ve got constant pain from my pancreas. Could that be triggering it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, pain and stress are both possible triggers. Your history of chronic pancreatitis and diabetes makes this complex. We’re coordinating with GI and endocrinology to manage those too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had three ERCPs in the past for my pancreas. The last one, they took the stent out because the pain got worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see that in your record. You’ve been through a lot. We’ll make sure your pain is controlled while you’re here, and we’ll follow up with GI about your right-sided flank pain and possible gallbladder issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ve been using a lot of Dilaudid at home. I know it’s strong, but the pain is bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve noted that. For now, you’re on hydromorphone as needed, and we’ve added sustained-release morphine twice daily to help keep your pain steady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my insulin? I’m on Humalog twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll continue your insulin lispro—15 units twice daily. We’re monitoring your sugars closely, especially since gastroparesis can make timing unpredictable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. I sometimes throw up hours after eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why you’re on metoclopramide—helps speed up stomach emptying. Take it before meals as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. So what happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The EEG tech will come soon to place the electrodes on your head. You’ll be monitored continuously. Try to relax and get some rest. We’ll check on you often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How did you sleep? Any episodes overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I didn’t have any spells. But I did wake up with pain in my back and side again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see your nurse gave you hydromorphone at 04:30. Your labs this morning are stable—blood count and kidney function are okay. Glucose was 167 this morning, so not low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But it wasn’t high either. I usually check more often at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking it four times a day. If we see patterns, we can adjust. The EEG didn’t capture any events yet, but we’re still monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried nothing will happen while I’m hooked up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s frustrating, I know. But even if we don’t capture an event, that information helps. No seizure activity on EEG during an episode would suggest a non-epileptic cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like what? Panic? I don’t feel panicked when it happens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might not feel like typical anxiety. Some people have what we call psychogenic non-epileptic seizures—triggered by stress or trauma, but not from abnormal brain waves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Because of my PTSD?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. And your family history—your mom had epilepsy. That’s a risk factor, but it doesn’t mean you have it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re into day three. Still no episodes on camera or EEG. Your blood work remains stable. The neurology team is reviewing the data.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So does that mean I’m okay to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering it. The test didn’t capture your typical spell, so we can’t confirm it’s epileptic. But your exam is normal—no focal weakness, reflexes are present, and you’re alert and oriented.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still have the numbness in my hands and feet. That’s from diabetes, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s glove-and-stocking neuropathy—common with long-term diabetes. It doesn’t explain the spells, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure? I’m on lisinopril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We increased it to 10 mg daily. Your BP has been around 130/80—much better. That’s one thing we can feel good about.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to have a stroke like my mom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re doing everything we can to prevent that. Now, your wife called—she’s not feeling well. Is it okay if we discharge you a bit early?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no—is she okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: She said it’s not serious, but she needs to rest. She asked if you could come home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. I can follow up as an outpatient, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll schedule you in the epilepsy clinic. They may repeat the monitoring if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your discharge is approved. We didn’t capture your typical event on EEG, so we’re calling this a non-electrographic seizure disorder for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a real seizure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t say for sure. The brain didn’t show seizure activity, but your symptoms are real. It could be related to pain, low sugar, or stress. The epilepsy team will help sort it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most stay the same. You’ll take morphine 30 mg twice daily for pain, hydromorphone as needed, and continue your insulin. We’ve simplified some—duloxetine is now 30 mg daily, and omeprazole once daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the nicotine patch? I’m trying to quit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep using the 14 mg patch daily. Great step. Also, follow up with GI about your flank pain—could be gallbladder related.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate your time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself, monitor your sugars, and call if you have any concerns. See you in the epilepsy clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. And tell the nurses thanks too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ll pass that along. You’re cleared to leave whenever you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready now. Just need my things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers and prescriptions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I stop driving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given the episodes, yes, hold off for now. The epilepsy clinic will advise when it’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. I’ll take a cab home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. Stay safe, Mr. ___. We’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, the pain in my right side has been getting worse for three days. It’s sharp, constant, and I can’t eat anything without throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fevers or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt feverish and had chills, but no actual fever checked. And I passed out once in the bathroom—woke up on the floor, not sure how long I was out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your heart rate was very high and blood pressure low when you arrived, but it improved with fluids. We did an ultrasound and found your gallbladder is distended, but no clear signs of infection yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is it my gallbladder again? I’ve had this pain before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. Your symptoms overlap with your chronic pancreatitis. We’re going to do a HIDA scan to check if your gallbladder is functioning properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. The HIDA scan came back normal—your gallbladder is draining fine. That means it’s not acute cholecystitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the pain then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like an acute flare-up of your chronic pancreatitis. The pain pattern fits, and you’ve had similar episodes before. We’ll manage it with pain control and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I’ve been worried about those 'seizure' episodes. I passed out again last night, sweaty and shaky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the nurse called me. Your blood sugar was 34—very low. You responded quickly to dextrose and juice. That wasn’t a seizure—it was hypoglycemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I didn’t eat, so maybe that’s why. But it feels like I’m going to pass out every time my sugar drops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Because of your pancreatitis, your body doesn’t release glucagon well, which normally helps raise blood sugar. So you’re at high risk for severe lows, even without insulin errors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not epilepsy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Multiple EEGs in the past showed no seizure activity. These episodes are metabolic—low blood sugar mimicking seizures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. My mom had epilepsy, so I was worried it was genetic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Family history is important, but your tests don’t support that diagnosis. We’re adjusting your insulin to a sliding scale to prevent these lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did a CT scan of your neck because your parotid glands are enlarged. Any pain there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, they’re just swollen. I’ve had that for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scan shows no stones, infection, or tumors. It’s likely due to your chronic pancreatitis and diabetes—metabolic changes or repeated vomiting from gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing to worry about?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. We’ll keep monitoring, but it’s benign and common in your condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I was able to drink some broth without vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’re going to start you on oral intake slowly. Your blood sugar has been more stable since we switched to the sliding scale insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to pass out again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you don’t. We’re also sending you home with sustained-release morphine for pain and clear instructions on when to take it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my gallbladder? Should I get it removed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s an option. Since you still have gallstones and recurrent pain, you can discuss surgery with a surgeon. It might help, but it’s not urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll think about it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT neck results are back—no concerning findings. Your parotid swelling is still thought to be from your metabolic issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for checking. I was a little worried it was something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. But all signs point to your known conditions—chronic pancreatitis, diabetes, and gastroparesis—being the main drivers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well—eating, pain controlled, blood sugar in the 180s. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take all your meds as listed—especially the new sliding scale insulin. Call your diabetes doctor for follow-up. And if you want to discuss gallbladder removal, call the surgeon’s office.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel another low sugar episode?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check your blood sugar. If it’s low, take juice or glucose tabs. If you’re confused or can’t swallow, someone should give you glucagon and call 911.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks, Doctor. I feel much better knowing what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Take care, and follow up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hey, doc. I’ve had this bad belly pain for a few days. Started right after I ran out of my morphine. I’ve been using it for years for the pancreas pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And where’s the pain located?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Mainly in the upper right side, but it spreads across. It’s sharp, worse after eating. I’ve been nauseous and throwing up yellow stuff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I felt cold and shaky. My PCP said I was dehydrated and sent me here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve given you fluids and some pain medicine through the IV. We’re going to keep you NPO for now—nothing by mouth—to let your pancreas rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no food at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. We’ll reassess tomorrow. We also did an ultrasound of your belly to check your gallbladder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had stones before. Could that be it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound shows gallstones, but no signs of acute cholecystitis—so it’s not an emergency. Your lipase and liver tests are normal, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s my pancreas again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely an acute flare of your chronic pancreatitis, especially since you ran out of pain meds. We’ll manage the pain and get you rehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a few ERCPs before for stones. Do I need another?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Your ducts aren’t blocked, and there’s no sign of infection. We’ll focus on stabilizing you first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night showed a slightly low body temperature and an elevated anion gap.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt cold. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely due to dehydration and not eating. The anion gap suggests mild ketoacidosis from not taking in enough calories. We’re giving you fluids to correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ketoacidosis? Like in diabetes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but in your case, it’s from fasting, not high blood sugar. Your glucose was 148, which is a bit high but not dangerous. We’re monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take insulin. My routine got messed up when I got sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started you on a simple insulin plan—Lantus at night and a sliding scale before meals. It’s safer while we figure out your needs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked blood and urine cultures to rule out infection, since you felt feverish. So far, no growth, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Doesn’t look like it. Your temperature is improving, and you’re not showing signs of sepsis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain’s better. I’m really hungry though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’re going to try advancing your diet—start with clear liquids and see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go back on my regular pain pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart your oral morphine—30 mg every 12 hours. We’ll also give you the 15 mg tablets for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I need that to function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve kept down liquids and your pain is controlled. We’re going to switch you to a soft diet soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about my diabetes meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on the same insulin plan—5 units of Lantus at night and Lispro before meals based on your fingerstick readings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pancreas enzymes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll continue Pancrease and Viokase with meals. They help you digest food properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re ready to go home today. You’re stable, eating well, and your pain is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stick to low-fat meals, take your enzymes, and monitor your blood sugar. Call your doctor if pain worsens or you can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your PCP in 1–2 weeks. They’ll review your insulin and pain management. We’ve sent all your meds and instructions home with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I’ll make sure to follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. And remember—don’t run out of your pain meds again. That likely triggered this flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. I’ll set up a refill system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. We’re discharging you in good condition. If you develop fevers, vomiting, or severe pain, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest and take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers and prescriptions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Patel. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve got this bad belly pain, mostly in the upper right side. It’s been getting worse over the past week because I ran out of my pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You have a history of chronic pancreatitis, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve had it for years. I’ve had a few ERCPs done to help with the stones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And when did the pain get worse this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About a week ago when my morphine ran out. Then two days ago, I started feeling nauseous and threw up a couple times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you mentioned you went to your clinic today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, for a regular check-up. But I suddenly got really sweaty and shaky. They checked my blood sugar and said I was low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you were hypoglycemic. They gave you orange juice and sent you here. Did you lose consciousness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I stayed awake, but I felt really weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. You’ve been managing your diabetes with insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been taking my insulin like usual, even though I wasn’t eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That might explain the low sugar. We’ll adjust your insulin while you’re not eating much. Also, I saw you mentioned blood in your urine once?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, just once at the clinic. Haven’t seen it since. Worried me a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your urine, and it’s clear now. No blood or infection. A CT scan also showed no kidney stones or tumors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. What about the belly pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT shows calcifications in your pancreas, which fits with chronic pancreatitis. No new complications like abscess or pseudocyst.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s just a flare-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your white blood cell count is high, which suggests inflammation, not infection. We’ll keep you NPO for now—no food—to let your pancreas rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No food? How long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just until your pain improves. We’ll give you IV fluids and pain meds. Once you’re feeling better, we’ll start you on clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Can I still take my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, most of them. We’ll hold the metoclopramide since you’re not eating, but you’ll keep your insulin, blood pressure meds, and psychiatric meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take morphine twice a day—30 mg and 15 mg sustained release.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given you IV morphine for the acute pain. Once you’re stable, we’ll restart your regular oral doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, actually. Still some ache, but not as sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your labs are improving. Your lipase is normal, which is a good sign. We’re going to try starting you on clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have some broth or juice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with small amounts. If you tolerate it, we can advance to soft foods tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back — no growth, so no infection. That one episode of blood in the urine hasn’t repeated, so we don’t think it’s serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, that’s good to hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re also tolerating the soft diet well. We’re going to switch your pain meds back to your regular oral regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get the same doses as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart the 30 mg and 15 mg sustained-release morphine twice daily. Plus, we’re giving you 15 regular tablets for breakthrough pain—no refills, just to get you through the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. You’re eating regular food, pain is controlled, and labs are stable. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Any changes to my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No major changes. We’ve added a stool softener and senna for constipation from the morphine. And keep taking your insulin as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I follow up with my doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, see your primary care provider in a week. If you get fevers, severe pain, vomiting, or blood in urine again, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You should be out within the hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I worry about the cysts on my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT showed a few tiny spots, but they’re likely benign cysts. No need to worry unless they grow. Your doctor can monitor them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, please don’t stop your insulin, even if you’re not eating much. Just adjust the dose with help from your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be more careful about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep taking your pancreatic enzymes with meals—they help with digestion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I always forget those, but I’ll try to remember.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re important. They can reduce pain flares over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll stick to them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll also start you on low-dose aspirin for heart protection, given your diabetes and hypertension.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t take aspirin before—any side effects?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rare, but watch for black stools or stomach pain. If that happens, let your doctor know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, everything looks good. Nurse will bring your prescriptions and discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Stay hydrated, eat small meals, and don’t run out of your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. I’ve learned my lesson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your surgical team doctors. You're here today for your scheduled laparoscopic cholecystectomy, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wait, the appendix too? I didn’t know it was a problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're scheduled for 12:00 tomorrow. Tonight, we’ll keep you NPO after midnight—no food or drink. We’ll run some labs and get you prepped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my pain? It’s been pretty bad lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you're on long-acting morphine at home. We’ll give you IV pain meds tonight to keep you comfortable. It might take a little adjusting since you're used to higher doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, regular painkillers don’t do much for me. I’ve been on narcotics for years because of the pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve noted that. The team will monitor your pain closely and adjust as needed. Any allergies we should know about?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to several—Depakote, Keppra, oxycodone, Paxil, Zoloft, Bactrim, Seroquel. I’ve had bad reactions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, that’s already in your chart. We’ll avoid those completely. Your other conditions—diabetes, high blood pressure, gastroparesis—we’ll manage those too while you're here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My stomach’s been slow to empty, so I take metoclopramide. Hope I can eat soon after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on clear liquids once your bowels wake up. Most patients tolerate that by the second day. We’ll also restart your pancreatic enzymes—Viokase—with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. How bad was the pain in my belly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugar? I’m on insulin.

conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve kept down apple juice and broth. We’re advancing your diet to regular food for lunch.

conversation_lines.text: Really? I can eat solid food already?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ve learned the hard way not to skip those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain now? On a scale of 1 to 10?

conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And driving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. Follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Rest, stay hydrated, and call if anything seems off. Take care.
