conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No stones or blockages?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had enough with pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.text: So why did I pass out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be here long?

conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning are better. White count is coming down, no signs of infection. We’re going to start you on your regular meds by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Any warning signs I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the hallucinations?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.text: Will I need another MRI or CT soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my back pain? It’s been acting up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my cholesterol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: Given the syncopal episode and possible pseudoseizures, yes—follow up with them. They may want to adjust your management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ll make the call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. We’ll send your discharge papers and prescriptions to your pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. I just want to feel normal again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Patel. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had this terrible belly pain for the last two days. It started after I ate a big meal with fried chicken. Then I got sick—nausea, vomiting, loose stools. Feels just like my old pancreatitis flare-ups, but worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You made it through the night without vomiting. That’s a good sign. We’re going to try you on a clear liquid diet.

conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I’m really hungry.

conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about my other meds? I take a lot for my bipolar and nerves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want anything messing with my mood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You kept down apple juice and broth. We’re upgrading you to a low-fat solid diet—small portions, no oils or fried foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have toast? Maybe some plain chicken?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Lesson learned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re walking around, eating, and your pain is much better. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.text: Continue the low-fat diet. Take your pancreatic enzymes with every meal—they help digest food and reduce strain on your pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking those, but sometimes I forget.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Try to be consistent. We’re switching to a different brand that’s easier to take—two tablets with each meal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home today. We’re giving you a short supply of Dilaudid for breakthrough pain, but use it sparingly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your gastroenterologist. If you can’t keep fluids down, have a fever, or severe pain, come back to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my 'seizures'—should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They seem tied to pain. If you can control the pain, they’ll likely stop. But mention them at your neurology follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, follow up with your PCP and GI doctor, and avoid alcohol and fatty foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been sober for years. I know what triggers this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. Keep it up. We’re also adding a stool softener and senna to prevent constipation from the pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take them as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re alert, walking, and eating well. We’ll get your discharge papers ready, and you should be out by noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my back pain. It’s been acting up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted your chronic back pain. It’s likely separate from the pancreatitis. Keep using your usual pain strategies, and follow up with your pain clinic if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I just wanted to make sure it wasn’t something new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All part of your care. We’re addressing everything together.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Here’s your discharge summary and prescriptions. You’re doing great. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the help. I’ll follow up with my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Stay hydrated, eat small low-fat meals, and call if anything worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you today. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. I was worried something was really wrong up there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did a CT of your abdomen. It shows changes from chronic pancreatitis—pancreatic atrophy and calcifications—but no new blockages or acute issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s just another flare-up? I’ve had so many of these.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely triggered by the fatty meal. We’re going to keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now to let your pancreas rest. You’ll get fluids and pain meds through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I have to stay like this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually a day or two, until your pain improves and we can start you on a clear diet. We’ll advance it slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m back to check on you. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but better since the IV meds. I’m really worried about the weight loss though—I’ve lost about 40 pounds in three weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s significant. It’s likely from not eating well due to pain and nausea. We’ll work on getting your nutrition back on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also had a high blood sugar at home—470. I have diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. Your glucose was 158 when you arrived. We’re monitoring it and will use a sliding scale insulin to keep it under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to end up in trouble with that again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your lab results. Your white blood cell count is a bit high—13.9—which suggests inflammation, not infection. Your lipase is normal, which supports this being a chronic flare, not acute pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.text: What about the acidosis they mentioned in triage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s because I’m not eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I have broth or juice?

conversation_lines.text: Yes, things like that. We’ll advance to a full liquid diet, then low-fat solids if you do well. No fatty foods—those are a trigger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well on the clear diet. We’re switching your pain meds from IV to oral. You’ll get oxycodone 15 mg twice a day with 5 mg for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that stronger than what I was taking at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a structured plan to manage your pain safely. We’re also keeping your other meds—like duloxetine, lisinopril, and simvastatin—on schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What should I do when I get home?

conversation_lines.text: And if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.text: We’re here to support you. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been sober for years. I won’t touch alcohol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. Keep up the good work. Call your doctor if pain worsens or you can’t keep food down. Otherwise, see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see how you do after the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another admission for the ERCP?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s outpatient. You’ll go in, they’ll remove the stones, and you’ll go home the same day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds better than being here again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Agreed. Just rest, take your meds, and wait for their call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my back pain? It’s still there, but not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw a small hemangioma in your L2 vertebra on the MRCP, but it’s benign and not causing issues. Your chronic back pain is separate—keep managing it as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. You’re doing well. Let’s get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team doctors. You've been admitted for severe abdominal pain. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, the pain in my upper belly’s been getting worse over the past few days. It’s sharp, comes and goes, but lately it hasn’t let up. I’ve also been nauseous and threw up a couple times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Given your history of chronic pancreatitis, this sounds like another flare-up. We’ll run some tests, but it looks like acute on chronic pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it because of those stones again? Last time they said the duct was blocked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your recent MRCP showed two stones in the pancreatic duct—one in the neck and one in the mid-body. They’re causing a blockage, and the duct has widened from 4mm to 10mm. That’s likely why the pain is so severe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the plan? More ERCP? Last time the stent made things worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not doing another ERCP this time. Because of your history and the size of the stones, the team is planning a Puestow procedure—a surgery to drain the pancreas. It’s scheduled for next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Surgery? I thought we could just remove the stones like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We could try, but you’ve had multiple ERCPs already, and the stones keep coming back. The Puestow will create a permanent drainage path, which should help prevent future flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about pain now? It’s really bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, you’re getting IV fluids and Dilaudid through a PCA pump—press the button when you need it. We switched from regular IV doses because the PCA gives better control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I pressed it a few times. It’s helping, but not completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Give it a little time. We’ll keep monitoring. We also started you on omeprazole to protect your stomach and pancreatic enzymes with meals to help digestion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on those already at home. Should I keep taking duloxetine and lisinopril?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve continued all your home meds except painkillers—we’re managing that here. Your blood pressure and mood meds are important to keep stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable. The lipase was low on admission, but that’s common in chronic cases. Your glucose is 188, so we’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that high? I have diabetes, but I thought I had it under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a bit elevated, but not dangerous. Stress and illness can raise blood sugar. We’re not starting insulin—you’re tolerating sips, and we’ll advance your diet slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat real food soon? I’m tired of just sipping water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to move you to clear liquids today. If you tolerate that, tomorrow you can start a low-fat diet. Pancreatitis means we have to go slow with food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Low-fat, right. I remember from last time. No fried stuff, no heavy meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And keep taking your pancreatic enzymes with every meal—they help your body digest food properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well—no vomiting, pain is better with oral meds now. We’re switching you from the PCA to oral Dilaudid as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I don’t like the IV thing anyway. Can I walk around more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please do. Ambulating helps prevent blood clots, especially since you have a history of DVT. We’ve been giving you heparin shots and you’ve been using the compression boots—great job.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last hospital stay. I’ll keep walking the hall a few times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We also did a chest X-ray today as part of your pre-op workup. It came back normal, which is good before surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is everything looking okay for the surgery next week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. ECG was normal, labs are stable, and you’re moving your bowels and urinating normally. All signs point to you being ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re being discharged today. You’ve been on a low-fat diet, pain is controlled with oral meds, and you’re walking well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do before surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Resume all your regular medications except NSAIDs—no ibuprofen, naproxen, or aspirin. They can increase bleeding risk. Take omeprazole, simvastatin, and your other meds as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the Dilaudid? I still have some pain at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re getting a 30-day supply with no refills. Use it only as needed. Also, we’re adding Colace for constipation, which can happen with pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it easy, rest, and keep walking. No driving, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Don’t drive or operate heavy machinery while on pain meds. And avoid lifting anything heavy until your surgeon clears you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll follow up with my PCP and the surgeon. Is there anything else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just stay hydrated, keep eating low-fat, and call if you develop fever, severe pain, or vomiting. Otherwise, see you next week for surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. I appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You’ve done really well. Take care, and we’ll see you soon for the Puestow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. You're here today for your Puestow procedure to help with your chronic pancreatitis pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks. I’ve been having a lot of pain lately, especially in the middle of my belly. Is this surgery going to fix that?

conversation_lines.text: I remember having stones before. They took them out with a scope, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Will I be asleep the whole time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m starving. Can I have broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, clear broth is perfect. We’ll see how you tolerate it and move to soft foods tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the catheter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s already out. You’ve been able to urinate on your own, which is great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray shows some dilated bowel loops. This is common after surgery — it’s called an ileus. It means your gut is still waking up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not usually. We’re encouraging you to walk and use the incentive spirometer to help everything get moving. It should resolve in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Aspiration? How did that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes after surgery, especially with sedation, stomach contents can go into the lungs. It’s not uncommon. We’ll monitor it and make sure it clears.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the lymph node?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be reactive from infection or inflammation. But we recommend a bronchoscopy later to rule out anything serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a brief episode yesterday that looked like a seizure. Neurology was consulted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t remember that. Was it a real seizure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Neurology thinks it was a nonepileptic event, similar to pseudoseizures you’ve had before. They don’t recommend more testing. Psychiatry thinks the confusion was from the narcotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my epilepsy acting up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you’re still on your seizure meds, but this wasn’t a true seizure. We’re tapering the narcotics, and your mental clarity has improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I feel much more like myself today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. You’re on a regular diet, walking without help, and your pain is controlled with oral hydromorphone and gabapentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. We’ll send you home with pain meds, Viokase for digestion, and a nicotine patch since you’re trying to quit smoking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll resume all your home medications — lisinopril, simvastatin, ziprasidone, omeprazole, and the others — unless we say otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the gabapentin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take it at bedtime for four days to help with nerve pain and then stop. We’re also giving you a short supply of hydromorphone for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final plan: You’ll be discharged tomorrow morning. A home health nurse will check on you, and you’ll follow up with me and your PCP in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you have increasing pain, redness or drainage from the incision, fever, or trouble breathing. No heavy lifting for a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I shower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can shower. Gently wash the area and pat it dry. No baths or swimming until your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And driving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not while on pain meds. Wait until you’re off them and cleared by your surgeon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll take it slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. You’re alert, eating well, and your vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember to rest, keep walking, and follow up with your doctors. The home health nurse will visit tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. And I’ll schedule the bronchoscopy soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Take care, and call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. The pain is unbearable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started IV fluids and pain medication. You’re also getting anti-nausea medicine. For now, we’re keeping you NPO—nothing by mouth—to let your pancreas rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll reassess tomorrow. If your pain improves and you can tolerate food, we might discharge you the next day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Can I eat something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other meds? I take Cymbalta, gabapentin, Geodon…

conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about the nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well today. You kept down apple juice and broth, and your pain is much better. We think you’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I feel so much better. I’m glad I don’t have to stay longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll send you home with pain meds, omeprazole, and your pancreatic enzymes. Take the Zofran only if nausea returns. And follow up with your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll make sure to take it easy and eat small meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And if you have severe pain, vomiting, or pass out again, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to go through this again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And no more passing out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been on regular food for a few hours with no nausea or pain flare. We’re comfortable discharging you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great! I can see my kids for Father’s Day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my enzyme pills for the pancreas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep taking those with meals. And follow up with your primary doctor and Community Counseling. They’ll get your records from this stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, eat small meals, and call if the pain comes back or you pass out again. Have a great Father’s Day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.text: So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not going to need surgery or anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
