conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. Surgery has been consulted before and agrees there’s no need for intervention now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. But I do pass out sometimes when the pain gets really bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you mentioned that. And you become incontinent during those episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, both urine and stool. It only happens when I’m in extreme pain and I bear down hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your history. These episodes have been evaluated before, and they’re likely related to your chronic pain and possibly pseudoseizures, not a true seizure or heart issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not life-threatening, but we’ll keep monitoring. Your ECG was normal—sinus rhythm, no changes from before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but maybe a little less intense. I haven’t thrown up since last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’re going to try advancing your diet—start with clear liquids and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m hungry. Can I have water or broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with that. If you tolerate it, we’ll move to solid food later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with the liquids. You’ve had a small meal and kept it down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I had some crackers and applesauce. No nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to switch your pain meds from IV to oral Dilaudid so you can take it by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I’d rather not have the IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your pain has improved, and you’ve been eating and moving around. We’d like to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about my insulin? I was worried about my sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Since you weren’t eating much, we reduced your Lantus from 10 to 5 units at bedtime. Please keep it at 5 units when you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, so half my usual dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And follow up with your doctor soon to adjust it based on your eating and blood sugar levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Should I restart my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your usual medications—omeprazole, metoclopramide, the pancreatic enzymes, lisinopril, simvastatin, and aspirin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Amitriptyline for sleep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one at bedtime as needed. We also gave you a prescription for ondansetron for nausea if it comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. And if the pain gets bad again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Try your oral pain meds first. If it doesn’t improve or you can’t keep anything down, go to the ER or call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my hernia—should I see a surgeon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s being monitored. Surgery doesn’t recommend repair right now, but discuss it with your PCP for long-term planning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re alert, walking fine, and your vitals are stable. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I appreciate the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Keep your follow-up appointments, especially with your primary doctor for your diabetes and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And if anything changes, I’ll come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s the best plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my psych appointment is tomorrow. Should I still go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. It’s important for your overall care. Keep up with both medical and mental health follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had this bad stomach pain for a few days. It’s worse than usual. I was vomiting and my belly’s been bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned flailing and being combative earlier—was that part of the pain episode?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, when the pain hits hard, I kind of lose it. I don’t mean to. It’s like my body just reacts. I’ve had seizures before, but they think some are not real.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s helpful. We’ll keep that in mind. You also have a history of pancreatitis and a ventral hernia—is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had that Puestow surgery years ago. And the hernia’s been there a while. It’s been bulging more lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ve ordered a CT scan to check for possible bowel obstruction, since your symptoms suggest that might be happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bowel obstruction? Like my intestines are blocked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It could be partial—meaning not fully blocked—but still causing pain and vomiting. We’ll know more after the scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your CT scan is back. It shows a partial small bowel obstruction—your upper intestine is a bit swollen and dilated, but there’s no clear blockage point.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? Do I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Since it’s partial and you’re passing gas, we can try non-surgical treatment. You’ll be on IV fluids, nothing by mouth for now, and we’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds manageable. But what caused it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be related to scar tissue from past surgeries, or possibly your hernia. The CT shows the hernia is still there, but it’s not strangulated—good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the hernia didn’t cause the blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not directly. It’s unchanged from before. But we’ll keep an eye on it. For now, we’re treating the obstruction conservatively.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling? Any nausea or pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain’s better. Still a little bloated, but I haven’t vomited since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’re going to try reducing your hernia manually today—it’s reducible, so we can push it back in safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slow. You might feel pressure, but we’ll stop if it’s too uncomfortable. It could help relieve some of the strain on your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just completed the manual reduction. The hernia went back in easily. You did great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt pressure, but it wasn’t bad. My belly feels a little flatter already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ll keep you NPO a bit longer, but if you keep improving, we might start clear liquids tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The psychiatric team also stopped by. They reviewed your history of depression and suicidal thoughts. They recommend continuing your current mental health meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve been struggling with that. PTSD from old trauma, and bipolar. I’ve been sober for years, but the mood swings still hit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure your meds are adjusted properly. They suggested adding mirtazapine for sleep and depression—okay if we start that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve taken it before. Helps me sleep and eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news. You’ve been stable overnight, no pain, and you passed gas again. We’re going to start you on clear liquids—broth, apple juice—and if you tolerate that, move to a regular diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat solid food today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see how you do with clears first. If no nausea or bloating in a few hours, we’ll advance you. Your pancreas needs careful management, so we’ll go slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with the clear diet. We’re switching you to a regular diet. Start small—maybe toast and chicken—and let us know if you feel any discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m hungry. Can I take my pancreas enzymes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve updated your prescription to Pancreaze—three capsules with meals. It’s stronger than what you were on. Helps with digestion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, we’re adjusting some of your other meds. Simvastatin dose is lowered, and we’re adding haloperidol for mood stabilization, as recommended by psych.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Haloperidol? I’ve taken that before. Helps with the racing thoughts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And we’re keeping lorazepam available for anxiety, plus prazosin for nightmares—common with PTSD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve tolerated the regular diet, your vitals are stable, and your pain is controlled. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you start vomiting, can’t keep food down, or have worsening pain. Also, watch for fever, or if the hernia becomes hard or painful. Follow up with your surgeon and PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no heavy lifting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right—nothing over 10 pounds until you see the surgeon. Keep walking daily, stay hydrated, and take your meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to go home. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good. Thanks for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the surgical team. You're here today for your scheduled hernia repair, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been having a lot of pain near my old incision, and they said the hernia was starting to block things a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the imaging showed part of your colon was partially stuck in the hernia. We were able to reduce it, but because the defect is large, surgery is the best option to prevent it from happening again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will you be using mesh? I remember last time they did the Puestow, it was a big surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll be doing a primary repair with Prolene mesh overlay. It helps strengthen the area and reduces the chance of the hernia coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And how long will I be out after the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stay in the hospital for a few days. We’ll start you on IV fluids and pain medication, and gradually get you back on food once your bowels start working again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had gastroparesis before—will that be a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aware of your history. We’ll start you on clear liquids on post-op day one and advance slowly. We’ll also continue your pancreatic enzymes and monitor how you tolerate things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my diabetes—should I take my metformin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’ll hold metformin while you’re not eating and switch to insulin if needed. We’ll restart it once you’re on a regular diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, makes sense. What about my other meds—like for my mood and nerves?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll resume most of your psychiatric medications as soon as you’re able to take pills. The team will coordinate with psychiatry to make sure nothing is missed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had some PTSD flare-ups lately—work stuff, old memories. I hope I can sleep okay here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can help with that. You’re on prazosin and zolpidem at home—we’ll restart those as appropriate. Let the nurses know if you’re having trouble resting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from surgery. The procedure went very well—ventral hernia repair with mesh, no complications. You’re in the recovery unit now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks… I feel groggy. Is the drain in my side normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we placed a JP drain in your right lower quadrant to collect any fluid and prevent buildup. It will stay in until your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the catheter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s temporary. We’ll remove it tonight or tomorrow morning once you’re up and moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain’s okay right now. I see the PCA button—should I use it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, use it as needed. It’s hydromorphone, and it’s safe when used properly. We’ll switch to oral meds once you start eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs look stable. Glucose was 154 this morning—well controlled. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try some water or ice chips today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start you on clear liquids—water, broth, apple juice. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance your diet tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds—will I still get the PCA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep it for now, but once you’re on oral pain meds, we’ll discontinue it. Chronic pain service reviewed your case and recommended continuing gabapentin and adding acetaminophen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on a lot of meds—can you tell me which ones I’ll restart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart most: lisinopril, simvastatin, omeprazole, amitriptyline, ziprasidone, duloxetine, gabapentin, metformin once you’re eating, and your pancreatic enzymes with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the stool softener? I don’t want to strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll give you docusate twice a day and senna at night to help. Avoid heavy lifting for at least six weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling? Any nausea or pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain is about a 3. I had some broth and jello—no nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll upgrade you to a soft diet tomorrow—maybe mashed potatoes, applesauce. And we removed the catheter this morning—you voided fine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no problem. The drain is a little annoying, but I’ll manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re tolerating food well. We’re advancing you to a regular diet. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About a 4, but manageable. I’m on oral meds now—hydromorphone as needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and acetaminophen regularly. We discontinued the PCA. You’re walking well—great job with the ambulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I get discharged?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If all goes well today, we’re planning for tomorrow morning. You need to tolerate a regular diet, be pain-controlled, and have no fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be going home with the drain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’ll stay in until your follow-up. You’ll need to empty it daily, keep the site clean, and watch for signs of infection—increased redness, fever, or cloudy drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll take Keflex four times a day for 14 days to prevent infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve done well—afebrile, eating, walking, pain controlled. We’re discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about my staples?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll be removed at your follow-up. You can shower—just pat the area dry. No baths or swimming until then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And activity?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No lifting over 10 pounds, no driving while on pain meds. Continue walking daily. Follow up with surgery and your PCP in one week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I understand. I’ll take my meds, care for the drain, and call if anything’s wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re doing great. We’ll see you in clinic to remove the staples and drain. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had this bad belly pain since my hernia surgery. It’s not getting better. I’ve been throwing up and couldn’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned some dizziness or passing out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, twice at home. I felt really lightheaded first, then just blacked out. No injuries though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your heart rate was high when you came in—118. That’s likely from pain and not drinking enough. We’re giving you fluids through the IV to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was worried something was wrong with my heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your heart with an ultrasound—called an echo. It looks good. No blockages, normal pumping. Your heart is just responding to stress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. What about the pain? It’s still pretty bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan of your chest, belly, and pelvis. No sign of infection, blockage, or blood clot. The surgery site looks clean. We think this is a flare-up of your pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pancreatitis again? But I’ve been careful with my diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Surgery and stress can trigger it, even if you’re doing everything right. Your lipase was low, but your history and symptoms point to acute on chronic pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on IV fluids, control your pain with medication, and slowly restart your diet. You’ll start with clear liquids tomorrow if you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my meds? I take a lot of them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your home medications—like lisinopril, metformin, Creon, and your psychiatric meds. We stopped Keflex since surgery removed your drain and staples.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ve also had some watery diarrhea at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be from the pancreatitis or pain meds. We’ll monitor it. No signs of infection in your labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain’s a little better. I haven’t vomited since last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your heart rate is down to 92. That’s a good sign you’re rehydrating. We’ll try you on clear liquids this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have apple juice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, small sips at first. We’ll watch how you tolerate it. If no nausea, we’ll advance to soft foods tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. No vomiting after the clear liquids. I’m going to order a soft diet for lunch—like broth and applesauce.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. My belly still hurts, but less than yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching your pain med from IV to oral hydromorphone. It’s strong but safe for short-term use. Take it as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need it when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a small supply. But we’ll taper it quickly. Most of your pain should improve in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I have an update. The CT scan showed a small enlarged lymph node in your right lung area—about 1.7 cm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not clear yet. It could be from old infection or inflammation. No other signs of illness. I’ve notified your primary doctor to follow up with a repeat scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. I was scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll make sure it gets checked. No treatment needed now—just monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a good day. Ate soft food without issues. Pain is manageable. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if you keep doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue Creon with meals, avoid heavy lifting, and take it easy. Finish your pain meds only as needed. Follow up with your surgeon and primary doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the chest pain I had a few days ago—should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned left arm numbness and nausea? The echo showed no heart damage. Likely not a heart attack, but discuss it with your PCP. Risk factors like diabetes mean we should stay cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re ready to go home. You’ve tolerated a regular diet, pain is controlled, and your vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What about the lymph node?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ve sent a note to your primary care doctor. They’ll arrange a follow-up scan in a few weeks. Call if you develop fevers, weight loss, or cough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back to your normal list—metformin, lisinopril, Creon, gabapentin, and your psychiatric meds. You have a few days of hydromorphone for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to follow up. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in from the ER earlier today. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, doc. I’ve had this bad belly pain again—same as before. It’s in the middle, goes to my back. It’s been getting worse over the last few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned in the ER that you passed out twice because of the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, once I fell into the coffee table. Hurt my shoulder pretty bad. Didn’t hit my head, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked an X-ray of your shoulder. Good news—it’s not broken. Just some bruising. But we’re more concerned about the belly pain and the low blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sugars have been low. This morning it was 50. I took my Lantus after breakfast, but I didn’t eat much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That might be part of the problem. If you don’t eat a full meal, you shouldn’t take your Lantus. It can drop your sugar too low. We gave you D50 in the ER, and your sugar came up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I didn’t know that. I just take it every morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go over your insulin instructions before you leave. For now, we’re giving you IV fluids and some pain medicine to help you feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. The pain’s still pretty bad. Is it my pancreas again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like a flare-up of your chronic pancreatitis—what we call 'acute on chronic.' Your lipase was normal, but your symptoms and history fit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no gallstones or blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an abdominal X-ray. No blockage or free air. Just some increased gas, which can happen with pancreatitis. Nothing surgical.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had enough surgeries already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you’ve had the Puestow procedure before—that helps with drainage. We’ll manage this with fluids, pain control, and slowly restarting your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Just checking in. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Still sore, but not as sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. White count was high when you came in, but it’s coming down. That means the inflammation is settling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been monitoring it. It was 54 when you got here, but it’s been stable since. We held your insulin for now and are giving you small sips of juice to keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m hungry. Can I eat something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with clear liquids—broth, apple juice. If you keep that down, we’ll move to solid food tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about my Creon? I usually take that with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart that when you begin eating. It helps your body digest food since your pancreas isn’t working at full strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just got your morning labs back. Your lipase is 9—completely normal. Kidney function and liver tests are good too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So does that mean I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The pancreas isn’t actively inflamed right now. That, plus you’re keeping fluids down, is a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. If you tolerate a regular diet and your pain stays controlled, we could discharge you tomorrow afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I really don’t want to be here longer than I have to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But we need to make sure you’re stable. We also need to go over your meds carefully, especially insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You did well overnight—no vomiting, pain is mild. We’re going to try a soft diet: toast, applesauce, rice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m ready to eat real food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And we’ll restart your metformin soon—but not today. Your PCP wants to see you first, since it can upset your stomach when you’re recovering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll hold off. What about my Lantus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can restart it tonight—but only if you eat a full dinner. If you skip a meal, skip the insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done great. Ate breakfast and lunch without any issues. Pain is minimal. We think you’re ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking your Creon with meals, stay on clear liquids if your stomach feels off, and monitor your blood sugar closely. Hold metformin until you see your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Try your usual pain meds first. If it’s severe or you vomit, come back. But I think you’ll be okay if you rest and eat lightly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I’ll follow up with my PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself—and be careful with that insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick final check before discharge. Any dizziness? Nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel pretty good. Shoulder’s a little sore, but okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send you home with instructions and a list of meds. You’re cleared to leave whenever you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy. Rest, eat small meals, and call your doctor to schedule that follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Patel. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had this bad stomach pain for about four days now. It’s the same kind I’ve had before with my pancreas. But this time it’s going around to my back, left side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I see you have a history of chronic pancreatitis. Any nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve thrown up a few times. And… there was a little blood in it, just streaks. Not a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, chills, or trouble urinating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. And I haven’t had any issues with my urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright. Your vitals when you arrived showed a fast heart rate, but your labs came back normal. We gave you some fluids and medication for nausea and pain in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, the Dilaudid helped a little. But the pain’s still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to keep you on bowel rest for now—no food or drink by mouth—to let your pancreas calm down. You’ll get IV fluids and pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But what about the blood in my vomit? That scared me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely a small tear in the lining of your esophagus from vomiting. It’s called a Mallory-Weiss tear. It usually heals on its own, and your blood count is stable, so we’re not worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That makes sense. I’ve thrown up a lot before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did a chest X-ray to check your heart and lungs, since your heart rate was high. Everything looked clear—no pneumonia or fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I’ve had a lot of medical stuff over the years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see you’ve had several ERCPs and even a Puestow procedure. We’ll continue your regular meds for diabetes, blood pressure, and mental health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my metformin? Should I still take that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding it for now since you’re not eating. We’ll restart it when you’re back on a regular diet. You’ll keep taking your Lantus insulin at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my gabapentin and pancreas enzymes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart those once you start eating again. For now, we’re giving pain control with IV Dilaudid every few hours as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, I think. The pain’s not as bad. And I haven’t thrown up since last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your labs this morning are stable. No signs of infection, and your kidney function is normal. The flank pain seems to be gone too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, that’s better. I was worried it was a kidney stone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your urine, and there’s no infection or blood. So it’s unlikely. We think the flank pain was just referred from your pancreas flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. Can I try drinking something now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start you on clear liquids—water, broth, apple juice. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance to solid food tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the diet going? Any nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had some broth and gelatin, and I’m okay. No throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll switch your pain meds to oral—starting with something milder. No narcotics by mouth, but we’ll keep using the Dilaudid if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d rather not take strong painkillers if I don’t have to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re trying to avoid that. We’ll also restart your metformin and pancreatic enzymes with your next meal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. You’ve been on a regular diet since last night, no vomiting, pain is manageable. We’d like to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. But what should I do to avoid another flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stick to a low-fat diet, avoid alcohol completely, and take your pancreatic enzymes with every meal. Stay hydrated and keep managing your diabetes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had alcohol in years. But I know my diet’s been off lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be the trigger. Even small dietary lapses can set it off. Continue all your regular medications as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please schedule an appointment with your primary care doctor within the next week. Call us sooner if the pain comes back, or if you start vomiting again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You’re alert, walking fine, and eating well—so you’re safe to go home. We’ll send your discharge papers shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. You've been transferred here because of your hernia issue. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hey, doc. Honestly, I’m not great. The pain’s been getting worse, and I can’t keep anything down. I’ve been vomiting a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I’ve reviewed your records. You’ve had a history of chronic pancreatitis and a prior hernia repair. You noticed a new bulge in your abdomen a few months ago?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, right in the middle. It didn’t bother me much at first, but now it’s painful and I feel nauseous all the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you haven’t had a bowel movement in five days, though you’re still passing gas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. I’m worried something’s blocked or twisted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring that closely. At the other hospital, they placed a nasogastric tube and did a CT scan. It showed a loop of colon in the hernia, but no signs of strangulation or blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not dangerous right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not immediately. The bowel is still getting blood flow and isn’t obstructed. But because you’re vomiting and can’t eat, we need to manage this carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. What’s the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on bowel rest—no food by mouth for now—so your gut can settle. You’ll get fluids and nutrients through your IV. We also reduced the hernia manually earlier today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You pushed it back in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, gently. It was reducible, meaning it could be moved back into place. That’s a good sign. We’ll monitor to make sure it stays that way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started IV hydromorphone for pain. We’ll adjust it to keep you comfortable. You’ll also continue your regular medications, like metformin and lisinopril, but we’re watching your blood sugar closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on insulin at night. Lantus, 5 units.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve continued that. We’ll keep giving it at bedtime. Your diabetes is stable so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve also got PTSD and bipolar—been on amitriptyline and Cymbalta.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted those too. Mental health is important, especially in the hospital. If you feel anxious or overwhelmed, let us know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate that. I’ve had a lot on my plate—back pain, pancreatitis, now this hernia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We see that. But right now, our focus is the hernia. We’re not planning emergency surgery because there’s no obstruction. Instead, we’ll let your symptoms settle, then plan an elective repair.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I won’t be having surgery here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Once you’re eating and pain is controlled, we’ll discharge you to follow up with your surgeon for outpatient repair.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. How long will I be here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely a few days. We’ll start with clear liquids tomorrow if you’re not vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through the night without vomiting. That’s a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, feeling a bit better. Still some nausea, but not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to try advancing your diet to clear liquids—broth, apple juice. We’ll watch closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, small sips. We’ll increase gradually. Also, your chest X-ray yesterday was clear—no pneumonia or fluid. Good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had some chest pain last night. Was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely from the NG tube or lying flat. The X-ray shows your heart and lungs are fine. We’ll remove the NG tube soon if you keep tolerating liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I hate that tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get it out today. Your abdominal X-ray also showed no blockage, which supports our plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. You’ve been on a soft diet since last night with no vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I even had some mashed potatoes. Felt good to eat real food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ve stopped the IV pain meds and switched you to oral hydromorphone as needed. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Maybe a 3 out of 10 now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if this continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Discharge? What about the hernia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s still there, but it’s stable. You’ll follow up with your surgeon in about a week to schedule the elective repair.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on all your usual meds—metformin, lisinopril, amitriptyline, duloxetine, simvastatin, and omeprazole. Plus, a short course of hydromorphone for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take pancreasze for my pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve continued that—three capsules with meals. You’ll keep that up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared for discharge. We’ll get your prescriptions ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back if you start vomiting again, can’t keep fluids down, or if the pain gets worse or changes. Also, watch for fever, chills, or redness at the hernia site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And lifting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Avoid heavy lifting—nothing over 10 pounds—until after your surgery. Keep walking daily, stay hydrated, and eat a balanced diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks, doc. I’ll follow up with my surgeon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I restart my aspirin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve included it in your discharge meds—81 mg daily. It’s important for your heart health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And Colace for constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, twice a day. With the pain meds and recent bowel issue, it’ll help prevent straining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ve had enough trouble already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad we could help stabilize you. Recovery is ahead, but you’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again. I’ll take it one step at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best way. Nurse will go over instructions and get you discharged within the hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. I’ll be ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. You're here because of a recurrent hernia that's been causing you pain and vomiting. We're planning to repair it today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, doc. It’s been really bad lately—can’t keep food down, and the pain’s getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. The CT scan showed the hernia is trapping a loop of colon, which explains the nausea. That’s why we need to operate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it dangerous if we don’t fix it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it could lead to bowel strangulation—cutting off blood flow. That’s why we’re doing the surgery today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What kind of surgery is it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll repair the hernia through your old incision and place a mesh to strengthen the area and prevent recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had mesh before. Will it be the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Similar, but we’ll use updated material. You’ve had a few abdominal surgeries, so we’ll be careful with adhesions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my diabetes—will that affect recovery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your blood sugar closely. It’s important for healing, so we’ll adjust insulin as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from surgery. The procedure went well—repair of the incarcerated hernia with mesh. You’re in recovery now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long was I out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: About three hours. You’re on a PCA pump for pain—press the button when you need relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s sore, but I can handle it. Any complications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: None. The bowel was inflamed but not damaged. We’ll keep you on IV fluids and antibiotics for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray showed some atelectasis—partial lung collapse. We’ll have you use the incentive spirometer every hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not usually. It’s common after surgery. Deep breathing and early movement will help clear it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do it. Anything else I should know?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on clear liquids tonight if you’re nauseated. Also, you have a Foley catheter—we’ll remove it tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your white count is elevated at 17.7, but you’re not running a fever. We’re watching for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely. Surgery causes inflammation. But we’re giving you IV fluids and adding Toradol for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I try real food today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with clear liquids. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance to soft foods tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your catheter is out. Try to urinate on your own—let the nurse know if you have trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I’m feeling a bit dizzy when I sit up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal after surgery and from lying down. Sit slowly and let us help you walk later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You passed gas, which means your bowels are waking up. We’re advancing your diet to soft foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Can I stop the IV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Soon. Once you’re drinking well, we’ll remove it. Also, your chest X-ray improved—atelectasis is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching from PCA to oral Dilaudid, Tylenol, and Motrin. You’ll take them as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your incision has some redness, but no drainage. We’re starting you on oral cephalexin just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. The redness is mild—likely inflammation. The antibiotic is a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on a regular diabetic diet now and your sugars are stable. We’ve adjusted your Lantus and metformin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been walking a bit—feels better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Keep it up. We removed the JP drain this morning—no more tubes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If all goes well, tomorrow. You need to tolerate food, control pain with oral meds, and be mobile.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is coming down. The redness hasn’t spread. We’ll continue the antibiotic for seven days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I wear something to support my belly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll need an abdominal binder at all times for two weeks. It helps healing and reduces strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home today. You’re eating well, pain is controlled, and you’re walking independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What meds do I take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Resume all your usual meds—Lantus, metformin, lisinopril, simvastatin, etc. Plus, Dilaudid as needed, cephalexin for a week, and stool softener.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the binder?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Wear it constantly for two weeks. No lifting over 10 pounds. Showering is okay, but no baths or swimming.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I see you again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with your surgeon in one week. They’ll remove the staples. Call if you have fever, redness, or worsening pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I got kicked in the stomach by my brother a few days ago. Since then, I’ve had bad pain in the middle of my belly, and I’ve been throwing up—black and yellow stuff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
